title: The bird on a thread (Ascent 1.11)
hook: a bird tied by a thin thread can't fly any more than one tied by a cord

segments.voice: Yesterday, nada: nothing, nothing, nothing up the narrow path. Your line was nothing, then everything. Today, one of John's simplest pictures.

Things hardly worth mentioning. The phone, checked again and again. The grudge against one cousin. The need to be right in the group chat. The show that has to be finished tonight. A little pride in looking busy. Nobody would call any of it an addiction. Small stuff. Harmless. Thin little threads, really. John of the Cross has a picture for exactly those small things, and it isn't as gentle as it sounds.
screen: `THINGS HARDLY WORTH MENTIONING.` → `THE PHONE, THE GRUDGE, THE PRIDE.` → `THIN LITTLE THREADS.`

segments.voice: First, the bird. In the Ascent of Mount Carmel, John says it makes little difference whether a bird is tied by a thin thread or a thick cord. Either way, it can't fly. Sure, the thread is easier to break. But until it's broken, the bird is held just as firmly as if it were tied with rope. Second, what counts as a thread. John is specific, and surprisingly ordinary: being attached to a person, a piece of clothing, a book, a room, a certain kind of food, a bit of gossip, a small pleasure in knowing things. None of these are sins in themselves. What matters is the voluntary clinging, the grip we choose and keep choosing. He's not talking about the natural wants everyone has, which come and go on their own. He means the ones we hold on to. Third, the little fish. He borrows an old belief about a tiny fish, the remora, said to fasten itself to a great ship and slow it down. Small thing, big ship. The size of the attachment isn't the point. The holding is. Fourth, why he cares. John doesn't want us miserable. He says it's a pitiful thing to see people who have given up great things stay held by something small. A favorite cup. A grudge. So close to flying. Just one thread. And the image carries its own hope: a thread is far easier to break than a cord.
screen: `A THREAD OR A CORD, NO FLIGHT.` · `A BOOK, A ROOM, A BIT OF GOSSIP.` · `A LITTLE FISH HOLDS A SHIP.` · `SO CLOSE TO FLYING.` · then, large: `A THREAD STILL HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself, honestly and without shame, what small thing has a grip on you: not the big obvious ones, but the little one you'd never mention, a habit, a comfort, a grudge, a need to be noticed. Let it come to mind, and name it quietly, in one word. If you pray, show it to God and ask for help to cut it; if you don't, just picture the thread, and the scissors.
Remora. The tiny fish John also pictures, said to fasten itself to a great ship and slow it down, just as a small attachment holds back the soul. Today's word.
Your line: a thread still holds. Until it breaks, a thin one holds like a cord. That's two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics often use John's bird-on-a-thread image in examinations of conscience and Lenten practices, looking for small voluntary attachments rather than only for large sins.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: rewrote the hook so it no longer tells the listener what they believe ('most of us are pretty sure') or puts a number on their phone habit; the remora is now framed as an old belief John borrows; softened 'he's seen so many people' to John's own lament; ending now follows John (a thread is easier to break) instead of 'easiest thing in the world'.

Bird on a thread and the remora image: Ascent 1.11.4; list of ordinary attachments (a person, clothing, a book, a cell, food, gossip, small satisfactions): 1.11.4; natural vs. voluntary appetites: 1.11.2–3. All paraphrased; confirm.
'People who have given up enormous things and got stuck on something tiny' reflects John's lament in 1.11.4–5; paraphrased and softened. Confirm.
Ending line ('a thread is the easiest thing to cut') is our gloss; John does say the thread is easier to break.
